Hello again! I just wanted to write a small piece about another game that's been occupying my time: Rainbow Six: Siege. This game released with some controversy following the news that it would be dropping story mode to focus on multiplayer. Co-op campaign is one of my favorite things about Tom Clancy games in the past, so I was disappointed to hear the news. Despite that shortcoming, there are some good things to mention as well:

Game Modes

There are two main game modes in Rainbow Six: Siege. Terrorist Hunt, and Multiplayer. Both modes are similar, feature team-based combat, and utilize the same maps, so it's easy to switch between the two game modes without being thrown off.

In multiplayer, two teams of five square up in a game of attackers vs defenders, alternating between roles. The attackers are tasked with completing an objective (e.g. rescue the hostage, defuse the bomb) and the defenders are tasked with preventing the attackers from completing the objective. To keep things fair, the defenders are given thirty seconds of prep time to fortify and set traps for the attackers. Rather than having the attackers twiddle their thumbs during the prep time, attackers are given control of small camera-equipped drones that can search the operation zone for the objective. If the attackers locate the objective, it will be marked on their HUD when they breach the building, and that much easier to complete. If the attackers fail to locate the objective during prep time, they'll have to search for the objective when they enter the building.

Terrorist hunt is much like multiplayer, with a few minor differences. Instead of facing a team of five player-controller operators, your own team of five will face a much larger (~20) team of AI controlled enemies. Gameplay switches between attack and defense, just as it does in multiplayer. The other minor difference is the lack of prep time for the attackers. If you're defending, you still get thirty seconds to set up traps and fortify. If you're attacking, you can immediately begin your infiltration at the start of the match.

Having a constant objective is a nice break from the standard Team Deathmatch gameplay of other FPS titles, and I find myself enjoying both attack and defense in this game.

There is another single-player game mode called "situations," that exists mainly to teach you gameplay and characters, and provides an additional challenge for anyone who just wants to polish their skills in a single-player environment.

Operators

There are currently a total of twenty playable operators -- ten for the attackers and ten for the defenders. The attackers specialize in breaching and clearing, so most of their character abilities will aid in breaching walls and opening sight-lines. The defenders specialize in fortifying and placing traps to assist in defense. The operators come from five different specialist units: SAS (Britain), FBI SWAT (USA), GIGN (France), Spetsnaz (Russia), and GSG 6 (Germany); this doesn't have much effect on gameplay, but gives a nice background for each character in the unit. Your team will consist of different blends of nationalities each time you play.

Operators each possess a special ability that's unique to their character, and a small selection of weapons as well. Rather than picking your favorite weapon or ability, you may find yourself picking an operator that has a good mix of both.

Operators are fairly well balanced, and you'll often find yourself in a "rock, paper, scissors" situation where you'll have to rely on your teammates to deal with a specific defender or hold off a particular attacker. You won't often find yourself in a situation where an opponent's operator doesn't have a counter sitting on your team somewhere. For this reason, communicating with your team mates and keeping track of friendly movements is key.

Gameplay

The gameplay in all game modes is very team-oriented, so keep track of your squad. Weapon damage and recoil is closer to Counter Strike than Call of Duty, so expect to die a lot as you get a feel for each weapon and its capabilities. Because of the close-quarters environment of each level and the potential for ambush, 90% of the battle is often won before the first shot is fired. Whenever you encounter an enemy from around a corner, odds are good that at least one of you already knew the other was there; if that's not you, you're probably dead before you pull the trigger.

Rainbow Six: Siege is also unique in that you can destroy much of the level and carve your own path to the objective. Breachable walls and floors are something that Rainbow Six does incredibly well. There are a variety of surface types, and knowing whether you can break through a material is quite intuitive. Plywood and sheet rock are perfect for a breaching charge or shotgun-produced hole, while brick and concrete can't be breached or damaged. Because of the close quarters gameplay and the ability to reshape the level in a different way each match, it's tough to become bored with the number of levels provided.

Summary

Although I miss the co-op story mode of previous games, Rainbow Six: Siege feels like they dropped campaign in order to focus on a well polished muliplayer. The result is a compelling team vs team experience that may make you forget the lack of story mode. With two game modes and a variety of operators, Rainbow Six: Siege feels a more like Payday 2 than like Battlefront, offering more variety in a roster of twenty distinct operators and a style of attack and defense that's all its own.
